label: main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main}
    Let $\varepsilon, \eta > 0$. Let $\chi(x,D)$ be a pseudodifferential microlocalizer inside the cone 
    \[\{(x,\xi) \in T^*\mathbb{D}^2 \qquad \Theta(x,\xi) \leqslant (1 - \varepsilon/2) p(x,\xi)\}.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Then, there holds, for any $\lambda \geqslant 1$,
    \[\forall \delta \geqslant \lambda^{-1/3 + \eta}, \qquad \left\|P_{\lambda,\delta} \chi(x,D)\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb{D}^2) \to L^4(\mathbb{D}^2)} \lesssim_{\varepsilon,\eta} \lambda^{1/8} \delta^{1/8} \ln(\lambda)^{1/4}.\]
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $\varepsilon,\eta > 0$. For any $\lambda \geqslant 1$, there holds
    \[\forall \delta \geqslant \lambda^{-1/3 + \eta} \qquad \left\|P_{\lambda,\delta}\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb{D}^2) \to L^4(D(0,1-\varepsilon))} \lesssim_{\varepsilon,\eta} \lambda^{\frac{1}{8}}\delta^{\frac{1}{8}} \ln(\lambda)^{1/4}\]
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $\varepsilon,\eta > 0$, and let $\phi_{\lambda}$ be a $L^2$ normalized eigenfunction of $\Delta$ with eigenvalue $-\lambda^2$. Then, with $\chi(x,D)$ as in Theorem \ref{main}, there holds
    \[\|\chi(x,D) \phi_\lambda\|_{L^4(\mathbb{D}^2)} \lesssim_{\varepsilon,\eta} \lambda^{\frac{1}{12} + \eta},\]
    and thus
    \[\|\phi_\lambda\|_{L^4(D(0,1-\varepsilon))} \lesssim_{\varepsilon,\eta} \lambda^{\frac{1}{12} + \eta}.\]
head: environment

label: thmCdV
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thmCdV}
    For all $a \in M(\Omega)$, there exists a conic convex neighborhood $U\subset \mathbb{R}^2\backslash 0$ of $a$, and an open connected cone $C \subset \mathbb{R}^2\backslash 0$, and a canonical transformation $\psi$ from $\mathbb{T}^2 \times C \subset T^*\mathbb{T}^2 \backslash 0$ to $M^{-1}(U)$ such that 
    
    i. $\psi^{-1}$ sends the foliation $(\Lambda_a)_{a\in U}$ to the foliation $(T_\xi)_{\xi\in C}$, with $T_\xi = \mathbb{T}^2 \times \{\xi\}$.
    
    ii. There holds $p \circ \psi(x,\xi) = K(\xi)$, where $K$ is a smooth homogeneous function of order 1 on $C$.
head: environment
name: Colin de Verdière

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\Lambda \subset T^*\Sigma \backslash 0$ be a compact Lagrangian submanifold, let $\Pi : T^*M\Sigma\to \Sigma$ be the canonical projection, and let $\pi : \Lambda \to \Sigma$ be its restriction to $\Lambda$. Following \cite{golubitsky1980stable}, we say that $p\in \Lambda$ is singular if $d\pi(p)$ has a nonzero kernel, and we define $S\subset \Lambda$ the set of singular point. We recall that the {\rm caustic set} of $\Lambda$ is defined as $\pi(S)$. 
    
   \hspace{\oldparindent} Assume that $S$ is a submanifold of $\Lambda$ of dimension $1$. We say that $p\in S$ is of {\rm fold-type} if $ker(d\pi(p))$ and $T_p S$ span together $T_p \Lambda$. Finally, we say that $\Lambda$ has {\rm fold-type singularities} if all $p\in S$ are of fold-type.
head: environment

label: defregdom
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defregdom}
    Let $\omega \subset \Omega$ be a convex open conic domain of action-angle coordinates. In particular, let us write $\omega = \psi(\mathbb{T}^2 \times C)$, with $C$ an open convex cone in $\mathbb{R}^2\backslash 0$. Thus, $\omega$ is foliated by the Lagrangian tori $L_\xi := \psi(\mathbb{T}^2\times \{\xi\})$, with $\xi \in C$. For $\xi \in C$, write $S_\xi$ the set of singular points of $L_\xi$. We say that $\omega$ is a \textit{regular domain} if the following conditions are satisfied
    
    i. The curve $\{K = 1\}$ has everywhere nonzero curvature on $C$.
    
    ii. There is a finite number of directions, say $\mathbb{R}_+^* \xi_1,...,\mathbb{R}_+^* \xi_K \subset C$, such that, for all $\xi \in C \backslash \{\mathbb{R}_+^* \xi_1,...,\mathbb{R}_+^* \xi_K\}$, $\Lambda_\xi$ has fold-type singularities.
head: environment

label: defadapted
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defadapted}
    With the notations of Definition \ref{defregdom}, if $\chi(x,D)$ is a pseudodifferential microlocalizer supported inside $\omega$, we say that $\chi$ is \textit{adapted} to $\omega$ if
    
    i. There is an open subcone $C_1 \subset \bar{C_1} \subset C$ such that $\chi = 0$ outside of $\psi(\mathbb{T}^2 \times C_1)$.
    

    ii. There is a constant $c > 0$ such that, for all $i = 1,...,K$, $d(S_{\xi_i}, supp(\chi(x,D)) \geqslant c$.

title: Remark
body_md: This theorem doesn't cover Theorem \ref{main} since it would typically only apply away from the center and the boundary of the Euclidean disk $\mathbb{D}^2$. Hence, we give a direct proof in the case of the disk in order to include the center and the boundary in our estimates.

label: defJn
title: Definition
body_md:
For $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, we introduce the Bessel function
    \begin{equation}\label{defJn}
        J_n(t) := \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb{T}} e^{i(n\alpha - t\sin \alpha)} d\alpha.
    \end{equation}
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} If, for $k\geqslant 0$, we denote $\lambda_{k,n} > 0$ the $k$th zero of $J_n$, we recall that an $L^2$ orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions of the Laplacian with Dirichlet boundary condition on the disk is given, in polar coordinates, by
    \[\phi_{k,n}(r,\theta) = c_{k,n} \lambda_{k,n}^{1/2} J_n(\lambda_{k,n} r) e^{in\theta},\]
    where $c_{k,n}$ are positive normalization constants, and where the associated eigenvalue of $\Delta$ is $-\lambda_{k,n}^2$. Moreover, there holds $c_n \simeq (1 - \mu_{k,n})^{-1/4}$, where $\mu_{k,n} := \frac{|n|}{\lambda_{k,n}}$ is the radius at which the caustic set of $\phi_{k,n}$ is localized (see \cite{chabert2025infty}).
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
For $\textbf{n} = (n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4)\in Z^4$, we introduce
    \[\begin{split}
        C_{\textbf{n}} &:= \frac{1}{2\pi \Pi_{i=1}^4 c_{n_i}} \int_{\mathbb{D}^2} dx  \phi_{n_1}(x) \overline{\phi_{n_2}(x) \phi_{n_3}(x)} \phi_{n_4}(x) \\
        &=\int_0^1 r dr  \lambda_{n_1}^{1/2} J_{n_1} (\lambda_{n_1} r) \lambda_{n_2}^{1/2} J_{n_2} (\lambda_{n_2} r) \lambda_{n_3}^{1/2} J_{n_3} (\lambda_{n_3} r) \lambda_{n_4}^{1/2} J_{n_4} (\lambda_{n_4} r) \fint_{\mathbb{T}} e^{i(n_1 - n_2 - n_3 + n_4) \theta} d\theta.
    \end{split}\]

label: deftrisec
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{deftrisec}
    Let $\kappa > 0$. For $\textbf{n} \in T$, find 
    \[1 = \eta_{n_4}^{int}(r) + \eta_{n_4}^{caus}(r) + \eta_{n_4}^{ext}(r)\]
    a partition of unity of $[0,1]$ by smooth localizers $\eta_{n_4}^{\bullet}(r)$ (i.e. $0 \leqslant \eta_{n_4}^{\bullet}(r) \leqslant 1$) such that $\eta_{n_4}^{int}$ vanishes for $r \geqslant \mu_{n_4} - \frac{1}{2}\lambda^{-2/3 + \kappa}$, $\eta_{n_4}^{caus}$ vanishes for $r\notin (\mu_{n_4} \pm \lambda^{-2/3 + \kappa})$, and $\eta_{n_4}^{ext}$ vanishes when $r \leqslant \mu_{n_4} + \frac{1}{2}\lambda^{-2/3 + \kappa}$. Finally, we assume that 
    \[\left|\frac{d^k}{dr^k} \eta_{n_4}^{\bullet}(r)\right| \lesssim_k \lambda^{k(2/3 - \kappa)},\]
    where we stress that the implicit constant is independent of $\textbf{n}$.
    
    We define the trisection
    \[C_{\textbf{n}} = C_\textbf{n}^{int} + C_\textbf{n}^{caus} + C_\textbf{n}^{ext},\]
    where
    \[C_\textbf{n}^{\bullet} = \int_0^1 r dr \eta_{n_4}^{\bullet}(r)  \lambda_{n_1}^{1/2} J_{n_1} (\lambda_{n_1} r) \lambda_{n_2}^{1/2} J_{n_2} (\lambda_{n_2} r) \lambda_{n_3}^{1/2} J_{n_3} (\lambda_{n_3} r) \lambda_{n_4}^{1/2} J_{n_4} (\lambda_{n_4} r).\]

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\alpha > 0$. We define the set of $\alpha$-\textit{degenerate} zero sum sets by
    \[T_{\alpha} := \{\textbf{n} \in T \qquad \text{such that}\ \min(s(\textbf{n}), t(\textbf{n})) \leqslant \lambda^{1/3 + \alpha}\}.\]
head: environment

label: defregimes
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{defregimes}
    Let $\alpha > 0$, and let $\kappa > 0$ such that $\kappa < \alpha/100$. Then, there holds
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} i. For $\alpha$-degenerate zero sum sets,
    \[\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n} \in T_{\alpha}} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_2}| |a_{n_3}||a_{n_4}| |C_\textbf{n}| \lesssim_\varepsilon \lambda^{1/3 + \alpha} \ln(\lambda).\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} ii. More generally, for zero sum sets such that $\min(s(\textbf{n}), t(\textbf{n})) \leqslant \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}$, there holds
    \[\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\min(s(\textbf{n}), t(\textbf{n})) \leqslant \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_2}| |a_{n_3}||a_{n_4}| |C_\textbf{n}| \lesssim_\varepsilon \lambda^{1/2}\delta^{1/2} \ln(\lambda).\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} iii. For the interior estimate,
    \[\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n} \in T} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_2}| |a_{n_3}||a_{n_4}| |C_\textbf{n}^{int}| \lesssim_{\varepsilon,\kappa,N} \lambda^{-N}.\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} iv. For the caustic estimate, 
    \[\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n} \in T\backslash T_\alpha} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_2}| |a_{n_3}||a_{n_4}| |C_\textbf{n}^{caus}| \lesssim_{\varepsilon,\kappa,N} \lambda^{-N}.\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} v. Finally, for the exterior estimate, there holds
    \[\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n} \in T\backslash T_\alpha, \min(s(\textbf{n}), t(\textbf{n})) \geqslant \lambda^{1/2}\delta^{1/2}} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_2}| |a_{n_3}||a_{n_4}| |C_\textbf{n}^{ext}| \lesssim_{\varepsilon, \kappa} \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}\ln(\lambda)^{1/2}.\]
head: environment

label: univbound
title: Proof
body_md:
From the a priori estimate on the $L^4$ norm of $\lambda_n^{1/2} J_n(\lambda_n r)$ given by Lemma \ref{l4norm}, and applying Hölder inequality, observe first that
    \begin{equation}\label{univbound}
        \forall \textbf{n} \in T \qquad |C_\textbf{n}|\lesssim \ln(\lambda).
    \end{equation}

    \hspace{\oldparindent} Thanks to the bound \eqref{univbound}, we may prove the first two estimates of the proposition. Indeed, let us fix more generally $M > 0$, and let us write
    \[\begin{split}
        \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{s(\textbf{n}) \leqslant M} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_2}||a_{n_3}||a_{n_4}| |C_{\textbf{n}}| &\lesssim \ln(\lambda) \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{1 \leqslant s \leqslant M} \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n} \in T, \ s(\textbf{n}) = s} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_1+ s}| |a_{n_4 -s}||a_{n_4}| \\
        &\lesssim \ln(\lambda) \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{1 \leqslant s\leqslant M} \left(\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n_1 \in Z} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_1 + s}| \right)\left(\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n_4 \in Z} |a_{n_4-s}||a_{n_4}| \right)\\
        &\lesssim M \ln(\lambda),
    \end{split}\]
    where we apply the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality with respect to $n_1$ (resp $n_4$) to obtain that the sum on $n_1$ (resp $n_4$) is bounded by $1$ in the last inequality. 
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Similarly, we may write
    \[\begin{split}
        \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{t(\textbf{n}) \leqslant M} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_2}||a_{n_3}||a_{n_4}| |C_{\textbf{n}}| &\lesssim \ln (\lambda) \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{1\leqslant t\leqslant M} \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n} \in T, t(\textbf{n}) = t} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_2}||a_{n_2 + t}||a_{2n_2 + t - n_1}| \\
        & \lesssim \ln(\lambda) \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{1 \leqslant t \leqslant M} \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n_2 \in Z} |a_{n_2}||a_{n_2 + t}| \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n_1 \in Z} |a_{n_1}||a_{2n_2 + t - n_1}|\\
        &\lesssim \ln(\lambda) \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{1 \leqslant t \leqslant M} \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n_2 \in Z} |a_{n_2}||a_{n_2 + t}|\\
        &\lesssim M \ln(\lambda),
    \end{split}\]
    where we apply the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality with respect to $n_1$, for a fixed $n_2,t$, then with respect to $n_1$ for a fixed $t$.
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, apply this to $M = \lambda^{1/3 + \alpha}$ or $M = \lambda^{1/2}\delta^{1/2}$.
    
    \quad
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} With regards to the third estimate in the proposition, observe that is it enough to prove that, for any $\textbf{n} \in T$, and any $N \geqslant 1$, there holds
    \[|C_{\textbf{n}}^{int}| \lesssim_{\varepsilon,\kappa,N} \lambda^{-N}.\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, observe that, on the support of $\eta_{n_4}^{int}$, for any $N\geqslant 1$, Lemma \ref{expdecay} yields that
    \[\lambda_{n_4}^{1/2} |J_{n_4}(\lambda_{n_4} r)| \lesssim_N \lambda^{-N},\]
    where the upper bound is independent on $n_4$ and on $r$. Moreover, all the other quantities are bounded by a fixed power of $\lambda$.

title: Definition
body_md:
For $\textbf{n} \in T$, and $N$ large enough fixed, we introduce the coefficients
	\[\begin{split}
	&c_\textbf{n}^{ext} := \int_0^1 rdr \eta_{n_4}^{ext} \Pi_{i=1}^4 \cos\left(\lambda_{n_i}\left(\mu_{n_i} \alpha_{n_i}(r) - r\sin(\alpha_{n_i}(r))\right) \right) a_{n_i,N}(r) \\
	&c_\textbf{n}^{caus} := \int_0^1 rdr \eta_{n_4}^{caus} \Pi_{i=1}^3 \cos\left(\lambda_{n_i}\left(\mu_{n_i} \alpha_{n_i}(r) - r\sin(\alpha_{n_i}(r))\right)\right) a_{n_i,N}(r) \lambda_{n_4}^{1/2} J_{n_4} (\lambda_{n_4} r) .
	\end{split}\]

label: controlerror
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{controlerror}
	For all $\lambda \geqslant 1$, for all $\mathbf{n}\in T$, define, for $r - \mu_{n_4} \gtrsim \lambda^{-2/3 + \kappa}$,
	\[a_{err}(r, \mathbf{n}, \lambda) := e^{i e(\lambda,r,\boldsymbol{\nu})},\]
	where the error term $e$ is defined by equation \eqref{deferrorterm}. Then, there holds
	\[ \left| \frac{d^K}{dr^K} a_{err}(r,\mathbf{n},\lambda)\right| \lesssim_{\kappa} (r-\mu_{n_4})^{-K}.\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
One needs only prove the bound
\[\left|\frac{d^k}{dr^k} e(\lambda,r,\boldsymbol{\nu})\right|\lesssim_{\kappa} (r-\mu_{n_4})^{-k}.\]
\hspace{\oldparindent} Now, for any $i$,
\[\left|\frac{d^k}{dr^k} \left(\lambda_{n_i} f(r,\mu_{n_i}) - \lambda f(r,\nu_i)\right)\right| \lesssim |\lambda - \lambda_{n_i}| \left|\frac{d^k}{dr^k} f(r,\mu_{n_i})\right| + \lambda \left|\frac{d^k}{dr^k} f(r,\mu_{n_i}) - \frac{d^k}{dr^k} f(r,\nu_i)\right|.\]

\hspace{\oldparindent} From the explicit expression of $f$, one finds that, for any $r \gtrsim \nu + \lambda^{-2/3 +\kappa}$,
\[\left|\frac{d^k}{dr^k} f(r,\nu)\right| \lesssim (r-\nu)^{3/2 - k},\]
and
\[\left|\frac{d}{d\nu} \frac{d^k}{dr^k} f(r,\nu)\right| \lesssim (r-\nu)^{1/2 - k}.\] 

\hspace{\oldparindent} In particular, we may further bound
\[\left|\frac{d^k}{dr^k} f(r,\mu_{n_i}) - \frac{d^k}{dr^k} f(r,\nu_i)\right| \lesssim \lambda |\mu_{n_i} - \nu_i| (r-\mu_{n_i})^{1/2 - k} \lesssim (r-\mu_{n_i})^{1/2-k}.\]

label: uncertainty
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{uncertainty}
    Let $\textbf{n} \in T$. If
    \[s(\textbf{n}) b(\textbf{n}) \gtrsim \lambda \delta, \]
    then there actually holds
    \[s(\textbf{n}) b(\textbf{n}) \gtrsim \lambda.\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} As a corollary, the following spacing version holds : let $n_1', n_4' \in Z$ such that $\textbf{n}' = (n_1', n_2, n_3, n_4') \in T$, and such that $\sigma := s(\textbf{n}') - s(\textbf{n}) > 0$. Then, if 
    \[\sigma b(\textbf{n}) \gtrsim \lambda \delta,\]
    there holds 
    \[\sigma b(\textbf{n}) \gtrsim \lambda.\]
head: environment

label: lattice
title: Proof
body_md:
First, assume that we can prove that, for $i=1,2,3,4$, there exists an integer $m_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that
    \begin{equation}\label{lattice}
        f(1,\nu_i) = \frac{m_i + 1/2}{\lambda} \pi + O(\delta \lambda^{-1}).
    \end{equation}
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Then, fix 
    \[g(\nu) = -f(1,\nu) = \sqrt{1 - \nu^2} - \nu \arccos(\nu),\]
    which is a strictly convex function on $[\varepsilon,1 - \varepsilon]$ (it is a primitive of $-\arccos(\nu)$). We may thus write
    \[s(\boldsymbol{\nu})b(\boldsymbol{\nu}) \gtrsim M_g(\boldsymbol{\nu}) = \frac{m_2 + m_3 - m_1 - m_4}{\lambda} \pi + O(\delta \lambda^{-1}).\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, if we assume that $s(\textbf{n}) b(\textbf{n}) \geqslant C\lambda \delta$ for $C> 0$ a large enough constant which doesn't depend on $\textbf{n}$ or $\lambda,\delta$, the left-hand side is strictly larger than the remainder in the right-hand side of the equation. In particular, $m_2 + m_3 - m_1 - m_4$ cannot vanish. Since it is an integer, it is thus larger than $1$, and we may finally write
    \[s(\boldsymbol{\nu}) b(\boldsymbol{\nu}) \gtrsim \lambda^{-1},\]
    which is equivalent to the result.
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} We now turn to the proof of \eqref{lattice}. Let us fix, more generally, any $n \in Z$. Applying Lemma \ref{Lemmstatphase} for $N = 1$ and $r = 1$, we find that, since $J_n(\lambda_n) = 0$ by definition,
    \[\frac{\cos(\lambda_n f(1, \mu_n))}{(1 - \mu_n^2)^{1/4}} a_{n,1}(1,\mu_n) = O(\lambda^{-1}),\]
    which we may rewrite, since $1 - \mu_n \geqslant \varepsilon$, as
    \[\cos(\lambda_n f(1, \mu_n)) = O(\lambda^{-1}).\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} In particular, this ensures that there exists $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that
    \[\lambda_n f(1, \mu_n) = (m + 1/2) \pi + O(\lambda^{-1}).\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, letting $\nu = n/\lambda$, we may rewrite that
    \[\lambda_n f(1, \mu_n) = (\lambda+O(\delta))f(1, \nu + O(\delta \lambda^{-1})) = \lambda f(1,\nu) + O(\delta),\]
    and thus, dividing the equality by $\lambda$,
    \[f(1,\nu) = \frac{m+1/2}{\lambda} \pi + O(\delta \lambda^{-1}).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us first write
    \[\begin{split}
        \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{s(\textbf{n}) \gtrsim \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}} |a_{n_1}||a_{n_2}||a_{n_3}||a_{n_4}| \frac{\lambda}{s(\textbf{n}) b(\textbf{n})} &\leqslant \left(\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n} \in T} |a_{n_1}|^2 |a_{n_3}|^2 |a_{n_4}|^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n}\in T, s(\textbf{n}) \gtrsim \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}} |a_{n_2}|^2 \frac{\lambda^2}{s(\textbf{n})^2 b(\textbf{n})^2}\right)^{1/2} \\
        &\leqslant \left(\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n}\in T, s(\textbf{n}) \gtrsim \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}} |a_{n_2}|^2 \frac{\lambda^2}{s(\textbf{n})^2 b(\textbf{n})^2}\right)^{1/2}.
    \end{split}\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, let us first compute the sum when $n_2,n_3 \in Z$ are fixed. In particular, the top of any zero sum set with second and third coordinates $n_2$, $n_3$ is fixed and equals $t := n_3 - n_2$. Moreover, each such zero sum set is determined entirely by its side $s\gtrsim \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}$, and its base is $2s + t$. Hence, we need to compute
    \[\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{s \gtrsim \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}} \frac{\lambda^2}{s^2 (2s + t)^2} 1_{(n_2 - s,n_2,n_3,n_3 + s)\in T}.\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} The interest is that we may now use the improved spacing for zero sum sets given in Proposition \ref{uncertainty}. Indeed, let us enumerate those zero sum sets $\textbf{n} \in T$ with fixed second and third coordinates $n_2,n_3$ by increasing side, say $s(\textbf{n}^{(1)}) < s(\textbf{n}^{(2)}) <...$. Applying Proposition \ref{uncertainty}, observe that, if 
    \[s(\textbf{n}^{(i+k)}) - s(\textbf{n}^{(i)}) \gtrsim \frac{\lambda \delta}{b(\textbf{n}^{(i)})},\]
    then there holds
    \[s(\textbf{n}^{(i+k)}) - s(\textbf{n}^{(i)}) \gtrsim \frac{\lambda}{b(\textbf{n}^{(i)})}.\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Thanks to this spacing fact, we may inductively partitionate the $\textbf{n}^{(i)}$ into clusters, in the following sense : find a sequence $1 = i_1 < i_2 < ...$, and denote $I_l := \{i_l \leqslant i < i_{l+1}\}$. Then, we may impose
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} i. Inside a cluster $i\in I_l$, there holds 
    \[s(\textbf{n}^{(i)}) - s(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)}) \lesssim \frac{\lambda \delta}{b(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)})}.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} In particular, the size of the cluster $I_l$ is bounded by $\max\left(\frac{\lambda \delta}{b(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)})}, 1\right)$.
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} ii. Moreover, between two clusters,
    \[s(\textbf{n})^{(i_{l+1})} - s(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)}) \gtrsim \frac{\lambda}{b(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)})}.\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} We claim that, as a consequence, for $l \geqslant 1$, and for any $i\in I_l$, there holds
    \[s(\textbf{n}^{(i)}) b(\textbf{n}^{(i)}) \gtrsim l\lambda.\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Indeed, let us prove this fact inductively. For $l = 1$, since we assume that $s(\textbf{n}^{(1)}) \gtrsim \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}$, then there holds
    \[b(\textbf{n}^{(1)} )s(\textbf{n}^{(1)} ) \geqslant s(\textbf{n}^{(1)} )^2 \gtrsim \lambda \delta.\]
    Thus, Proposition \ref{uncertainty} yields that $s(\textbf{n}^{(1)}) b(\textbf{n}^{(1)} ) \gtrsim \lambda$.
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, if this is true for some $l\geqslant 1$, write
    \[\begin{split} s(\textbf{n}^{(i_{l+1})}) b(\textbf{n}^{(i_{l+1})}) &\geqslant (\textbf{n}^{(i_{l+1})})b(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)})\\   &=(s(\textbf{n})^{(i_{l+1})} - s(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)})) b(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)}) +s(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)}) b(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)}) \\
    &\gtrsim \lambda + l \lambda = (l+1) \lambda.
    \end{split}\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} As a conclusion, and, since for any $l$ there holds $b(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)}) \geqslant t$, we may write
    \[\begin{split}
        \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{s \gtrsim \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}} \frac{1}{s^2 (2s + t)^2} 1_{(n_2 - s,n_2,n_3,n_3 + s)\in T} &\leqslant \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{l\geqslant 1} \frac{\lambda^2}{(s(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)}) b(\textbf{n}^{(i_l)}))^2} |I_l| \\
        &\lesssim \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{l\geqslant 1} \frac{1}{l^2} |I_l|\\
        &\lesssim \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sup_l |I_l|\\
        &\lesssim \max\left(\frac{\lambda \delta}{t}, 1\right)
    \end{split}\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Overall, summing finally on $n_2$ and $t$ yields
    
    \[\begin{split}
        \left(\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\textbf{n}\in T, s(\textbf{n}) \gtrsim \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}} |a_{n_2}|^2 \frac{\lambda^2}{s(\textbf{n})^2 b(\textbf{n})^2}\right)^{1/2} &= \left(\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n_2 \in Z} \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{t\geqslant 1} \displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{s \gtrsim \lambda^{1/2} \delta^{1/2}} \frac{\lambda^2}{s^2 (2s + t)^2} 1_{(n_2 - s,n_2,n_2 + t,n_2 + t+ s)\in T}\right)^{1/2} \\
        &\lesssim \left(\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n_2 \in Z} |a_{n_2}|^2\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{\lambda \geqslant t\geqslant 1} \left(\frac{\lambda \delta}{t} + 1_{n_2 + t \in Z}\right)\right)^{1/2}\\
        &\lesssim  \left(\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n_2 \in Z} |a_{n_2}|^2\left(\lambda\delta \ln(\lambda) +  \#Z\right)\right)^{1/2}\\
        &\lesssim(\lambda \delta \ln(\lambda))^{1/2},
    \end{split}\]
    since the cardinal of $Z$ is bounded by $O(\lambda \delta)$ thanks to the spectral estimate \eqref{improvedremainder}. This concludes the proof.

label: l4norm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l4norm}
    For all $n\in \mathbb{Z}$, for all $\lambda \geqslant 1$, there holds
    \[\left\| \lambda^{1/2} J_n(\lambda |\cdot|)\right\|_{L^4(\mathbb{D}^2)}\lesssim \ln(\lambda)^{1/4},\]
    where the upper bound is independent of $n$.
head: environment

label: eqappendixnorm
title: Proof
body_md:
Let us start by writing that
    \begin{equation}\label{eqappendixnorm}
        \left\| \lambda^{1/2} J_n(\lambda \cdot)\right\|_{L^4(\mathbb{D}^2)}^4 = 2\pi \lambda^2 \int_0^1 |J_n(\lambda r)|^4 r dr = 2\pi \int_0^\lambda |J_n(r)|^4 r dr.
    \end{equation}
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, using \cite{guo1997uniform}[Lemma 3.2], there holds, for all $p > 4$, and for all $n$,
    \[\left(\int_0^{\infty} |J_n(r)|^p r dr\right)^{1/p} \leqslant C(p-4)^{-1/p},\]
    where the constant $C > 0$ is independent of $p$ and of $n$. In particular, applying Hölder inequality to \eqref{eqappendixnorm}, we may write that, for any $\varepsilon > 0$,
    \[\begin{split}
        \int_0^\lambda |J_n(r)|^4 rdr &\leqslant \left(\int_0^\lambda |J_n(r)|^{4(1+\varepsilon)} r dr \right)^{\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}} \left(\lambda^2/2\right)^{\frac{\varepsilon}{1 + \varepsilon}} \\
        &\leqslant 2^{-\frac{\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}} \left(C (4\varepsilon)^{-\frac{1}{4(1+\varepsilon)}}\right)^{4} \lambda^{\frac{2\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}}\\
        &\leqslant 2^{-\frac{\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}} C^4 4^{-\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}} \varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}} \lambda^{\frac{2\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}}\\
        &\leqslant C' \varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}} \lambda^{\frac{2\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}}\\
        &\leqslant C' \varepsilon^{-1} \lambda^{2\varepsilon},
    \end{split} \]
    with $C' = C^4$. Now, the function $\varepsilon \mapsto -\ln \varepsilon + 2\varepsilon \ln \lambda$ reaches its minimum at $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2 \ln \lambda}$. For this value of $\varepsilon$, the upper bound reads
    \[\int_0^\lambda |J_n(r)|^4 r dr \leqslant 2 e C'\ln \lambda,\]
    from which the claim follows.

label: expdecay
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $r = 0$, observe that, for the condition $\mu_n - r > 0$ to be non empty, there must hold $n \neq 0$, and hence $J_n(0) = 0$. Now, assume that $r \neq 0$ and write
    \[J_n(\lambda_n r) = \int_{\mathbb{T}} e^{i\lambda_n r \left(\frac{\mu_n}{r}\alpha - \sin \alpha\right)} d\alpha.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, the phase function 
    \[\phi : \alpha \mapsto \frac{\mu_n}{r} \alpha - \sin \alpha\]
    satisfies
    \[\phi'(\alpha) = \frac{\mu_n}{r} - \cos \alpha = \frac{\mu_n - r}{r} + 1 - \cos \alpha \geqslant \frac{\mu_n - r}{r} > 0\]
    and all its higher order derivatives are uniformly bounded by $1$. Moreover, we claim that there holds 
    \[\left|\frac{\phi''(\alpha)}{\phi'(\alpha)}\right| \lesssim \max(1,\left(\frac{\mu_n - r}{r}\right)^{-1/2}).\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Indeed, assume that $\varepsilon := \frac{\mu_n - r}{r} \leqslant 1$. Then, for $\alpha \lesssim \varepsilon^{1/2}$, one needs only write that
    \[\left|\frac{\phi''(\alpha)}{\phi'(\alpha)}\right| = \frac{\sin \alpha}{\phi'(\alpha)} \lesssim \frac{\varepsilon^{1/2}}{\varepsilon}.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} For $\alpha \gtrsim \varepsilon^{1/2}$, one may instead use that 
    \[\left|\frac{\phi''(\alpha)}{\phi'(\alpha)}\right| \leqslant \left|\frac{\sin \alpha}{1 - \cos \alpha}\right| \lesssim \alpha^{-1} \lesssim \varepsilon^{-1/2}.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Thus, thanks to the above estimate, we see that, after integrating by parts $K$ times in $\alpha$, one may bound
    \[\begin{split}
        |J_n(\lambda_n r)| &\lesssim (\lambda_n r)^{-K} \left(\frac{\mu_n-r}{r}\right)^{-K} \left(\max\left(1,\frac{\mu_n - r}{r}\right)\right)^{-K/2} \\
        &\lesssim (\lambda_n r)^{-K} \left(\frac{\mu_n-r}{r}\right)^{-K} \left(\mu_n - r\right)^{-K/2} \\
        &\lesssim \lambda_n^{-K} (\mu_n -r)^{-3K/2} \\
        &\lesssim \lambda^{-3/2\kappa K},
    \end{split}\]
    from which the claim follows by choosing $K$ large enough depending on $N,\kappa$.

label: derlemm
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us start with the expression
    \[\frac{d^K}{dr^K} \left(\lambda^{1/2}_{k,n} J_n(\lambda_{k,n} r)\right) = \lambda_n^{1/2 + K} \int_{\mathbb{T}} e^{i\lambda_n (\mu_n \alpha - r \sin \alpha)} (-\sin \alpha)^K d\alpha.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, define the phase function
    \[\phi : \alpha \mapsto \frac{\mu_n}{r} \alpha - \sin \alpha.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Observe that $\frac{\mu_n}{r} = 1 + \frac{\mu_n - r}{r}$, where $\left|\frac{\mu_n -r}{r}\right|\lesssim \varepsilon := \lambda^{-\frac{2}{3} + \kappa} r^{-1} \lesssim \lambda^{\kappa - \alpha} << 1$. Thus, writing
    \[|\phi'(\alpha)| = \left|\frac{\mu_n}{r} - \cos \alpha\right| = \left| 1 - \cos \alpha + \frac{\mu_n - r}{r}\right|,\]
    we find that, if $C > 0$ is a large enough constant, for $|\alpha| \geqslant C\sqrt{\varepsilon}$, there holds 
    \[|\phi'(\alpha)| \gtrsim \varepsilon, \qquad \left|\frac{\phi''(\alpha}{\phi'(\alpha)}\right| \lesssim \varepsilon^{-1/2}.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Thus, if we define $\zeta(\alpha)$ a smooth localizer on $|\alpha|\leqslant C \sqrt{\varepsilon}$, such that $|\zeta^{(k)}(\alpha)|\lesssim \varepsilon^{-k/2}$ for all $k$, we may integrate by parts $M$ times on the support of $1 - \zeta$ to find that
    \[\int_{\mathbb{T}} e^{i\lambda_n r \phi(\alpha)} (-\sin \alpha)^K (1 - \zeta(\alpha) d\alpha = \int_\mathbb{T} O((\lambda_n r \varepsilon)^{-M} ) \varepsilon^{-M/2} d\alpha.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, write
    \[\lambda_n r \varepsilon^{3/2 M} = \lambda_n r \lambda_n^{-1 + \frac{3}{2}\kappa} r^{-3/2} \gtrsim \lambda^{3/2 \kappa}.\]
    
    \hspace{\oldparindent} In particular, as $M\to \infty$, we find that
    \[\frac{d^K}{dr^K} \left(\lambda^{1/2}_{k,n} J_n(\lambda_{k,n} r)\right) = \lambda_n^{1/2 + K} \int_\mathbb{T} e^{i\lambda_n r \phi(\alpha)} (-\sin \alpha)^K \zeta(\alpha) d\alpha + O(\lambda^{-\infty}).\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} To conclude, one needs only observe that, on the support of $\zeta$, there holds $|\sin \alpha|\leqslant |\alpha|\lesssim \sqrt{\varepsilon}$. Overall, we find that
    \[\left|\frac{d^K}{dr^K} \left(\lambda^{1/2}_{k,n} J_n(\lambda_{k,n} r)\right)\right| \lesssim \lambda_n^{1/2 + K} \varepsilon^{K/2}.\]
    \hspace{\oldparindent} Now, observe that
    \[\lambda_n^{1/2 + K} \varepsilon^{K/2} = \lambda_n^{1/2 + K} \lambda^{-1/3 K + \frac{K}{2}\kappa} r^{-K/2},\]
    which concludes the proof.
